lessons.title: Hello Java
lessons.summary: Classes, main, javac and java, statements and comments.

blocks.text: In Java, all code lives inside a **class**. The JVM starts your program by calling a method named `main`.

blocks.caption: Hello.java

items: `System.out.println` prints a value and then a line break.
Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
Curly braces `{ }` mark where a class or method starts and ends.

blocks.text: Python runs a file from top to bottom. Java needs a class with a `main` method. Indentation is only for humans: the braces define the blocks.

rows: The JVM can call it from outside
The exact name the JVM looks for

blocks.text: These variations are also valid entry points:

items: `String args[]` or `String... args` (varargs)
Any parameter name: `String[] x`
`final String[] args`
Modifier order can swap: `static public void main`

blocks.text: Not entry points: a non-`static` main, a return type other than `void`, a parameter that is not a `String` array, or the name `Main`. Some of these still compile, but `java` refuses to run them.

steps.prompt: Which two methods can be the entry point when you run `java Main`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Varargs `String...` is the same as `String[]`, and modifier order and the parameter name do not matter. A missing `static`, an `int` return type or a single `String` parameter means it is not the entry point.

rows: Runs the class; give the class name, not the file
Single-file mode: compiles in memory and runs; no `.class` file

items: A `public` class must live in a file with the same name: `Hello` goes in `Hello.java`.
`args` holds what follows the class name: `java Hello a b` gives `args[0]` = `"a"`.

blocks.text: `java Hello.class` fails (the JVM wants a class name) and `javac Hello` fails (javac wants the `.java` file).

steps.prompt: `public class Greeter` is saved in `Greeter.java`. Which command compiles it?
steps.explanation: `javac` takes the source file name with its `.java` extension. `java` (no c) runs a class by name, without `.class`.

steps.prompt: Put the lines in order to make a program that prints `5`.
steps.explanation: The class wraps the method, the method wraps the statements, and each brace closes in reverse order. `def` is Python, not Java.

blocks.text: Java is **statically typed**: each variable has a type that never changes.

blocks.caption: Prints Ada4

blocks.text: `#` is not a comment in Java. And unlike Python, a variable cannot switch from a number to a string.
Block comments do not nest: `/* a /* b */ c */` ends at the first `*/`, so ` c */` is left over and fails to compile.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `name` is a `String`, so it cannot hold an `int`. A variable's type is fixed when it is declared.
The last statement has no semicolon. The comment after it does not count. The comments themselves are fine.
`print` adds no line break. `println` adds one after its value. So you get `AB`, a line break, then `C`.

lessons.title: Primitive types & literals
lessons.summary: The 8 primitives, literal suffixes, number bases and defaults.

blocks.text: Primitives hold plain values, not objects. Know their sizes for the exam.
Python's `int` never overflows and its `float` is a 64-bit double. Java gives you fixed sizes, and `int` stops at 2,147,483,647.

steps.prompt: Which two are primitive types? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Primitive type names are lowercase keywords. `String`, `Integer` and `Long` are classes. `Integer` and `Long` are wrapper classes for `int` and `long`.

blocks.text: A whole-number literal is an `int`. A literal with a decimal point is a `double`.

items: `L` (or `l`) makes a `long` literal. Prefer `L`: `l` looks like `1`.
`f` or `F` makes a `float`. Without it, `3.14` is a `double` and will not fit.
`d` or `D` marks a `double`, but it is optional.

blocks.text: `long big = 3000000000;` does not compile. The literal itself is too big for an `int`, even though the variable is a `long`.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `2.5` is a `double` literal. Storing a `double` in a `float` could lose precision, so you need `2.5f`.

blocks.text: Underscores make long numbers readable: `1_000_000`. They are allowed **only between digits**:

items: Not at the start or end: `_100` and `100_` fail
Not next to `.`: `3_.14` fails
Not before a suffix: `99_L` fails
Not right after `0x` or `0b`: `0x_FF` fails
Several in a row are fine: `1__000`

blocks.text: A leading zero means octal. `int x = 017;` stores 15, not 17. And `09` does not compile.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Underscores must sit between digits. `_1000` is read as a variable name that does not exist. `3_.14`, `99_L` and `0x_FF` put an underscore next to `.`, a suffix or a prefix. `0b1_0` is binary 10, which is 2.
`0x10` is hex (16), `010` is octal because of the leading zero (8), and `0b10` is binary (2).

blocks.text: A `char` is a 16-bit unsigned number that maps to a character. `'A'` is 65.

blocks.caption: c + 1 is an int

items: Single quotes make a `char`, double quotes make a `String`.
`'AB'` does not compile: a char holds exactly one character.

blocks.text: Python has no char type: `'A'` and `"A"` are both strings. In Java, `'A'` is a number-like `char` and `"A"` is a `String`.

steps.explanation: `c + 1` is int math, giving 66. Casting that result back to `char` gives `B`.

blocks.text: **Fields** (variables in a class) get default values. **Local variables** (inside a method) get none.
Declaring a local without a value is fine. *Reading* it before it is surely assigned does not compile.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: The compiler does not run `y > 5`; it only knows `x` might not be assigned. Reading a local that might be unassigned is a compile error, so line 6 fails.

lessons.title: Operators & precedence
lessons.summary: Integer division, ++, compound assignment, logic and precedence.

items: `int / int` is an `int`: the fraction is cut off (toward zero).
The sign of `%` follows the **left** operand.
If either side is a `double`, the math is `double`.

blocks.text: Python's `/` always gives a float and `//` rounds *down* (`-7 // 2` is -4). Java's `/` on ints truncates *toward zero* (-3). Python's `-7 % 3` is 2; Java's is -1.
`Math.floorDiv` and `Math.floorMod` round toward **negative infinity** instead of toward zero. The sign of `floorMod` follows the **right** operand (the divisor).

blocks.caption: -9 / 4 is -2 but floorDiv gives -3; -9 % 4 is -1 but floorMod gives 3

steps.code:
int a = -7;
System.out.println(a / 2 + " " + a % 3);
steps.explanation: Integer division truncates toward zero: -7 / 2 is -3. The remainder keeps the sign of -7, so -7 % 3 is -1.

items: **Post**fix `x++`: the expression uses the old value, then x changes.
**Pre**fix `++x`: x changes first, then the new value is used.

blocks.text: Python has no `++`. In Java, `x++` both changes `x` and produces a value.
`x = x++;` leaves `x` unchanged: the old value is saved, `x` is incremented, then the old value is assigned back.

steps.explanation: Left to right: `x++` gives 3 (x becomes 4), then `++x` makes x 5 and gives 5. y = 3 + 5 = 8, and x ends at 5.

blocks.text: `x += 2` is not exactly `x = x + 2`. It includes a hidden cast to the type of `x`.

blocks.caption: 12.7 is cut to 12

items: Assignment is also an expression: `a = b = 4;` sets both to 4 (right to left).

blocks.text: For `short` and `byte`, `s = s + 1` fails but `s += 1` and `s++` compile.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `s + 1` is an `int` (short is promoted in arithmetic), and an int cannot go into a short without a cast. `+=`, `*=` and `++` include the cast for you.

rows: AND / OR, always evaluate both sides
XOR: true if exactly one is true

blocks.caption: Only & ran ++n

blocks.text: Python uses `and`, `or`, `not`. Java has no truthiness: `if (count)` does not compile for an `int`, and an empty String is not `false`.

steps.explanation: Line 2: `a > 5` is false, so `&&` skips `++b`. Line 3: `a < 10` is true, so `||` skips `++b`. Line 4: `|` always evaluates both sides, so b becomes 11.

blocks.text: `cond ? a : b` picks `a` if `cond` is true, else `b`.
`*`, `/` and `%` share a level and run left to right. On primitives, `==` compares values, after promotion: `5 == 5.0` and `'a' == 97` are both `true`.

steps.explanation: `*` and `%` bind tighter than `+` and run left to right: 4 * 3 = 12, 12 % 5 = 2, so y = 2 + 2 = 4. 4 is not > 5, so you get `small`.

steps.prompt: Fill the gaps so the code prints `true`.
steps.explanation: 7 % 2 is 1, so `a % b == 1` is true, and `a > b` is true. `&&` joins them. `%` binds tighter than `==`, which binds tighter than `&&`, so no parentheses are needed.

lessons.title: Casting & promotion
lessons.summary: Widening, narrowing, promotion to int, overflow and char math.

blocks.text: **Widening** (small type to big type) is automatic:
`byte` → `short` → `int` → `long` → `float` → `double`, and `char` → `int`.

blocks.caption: Casting a double to int truncates: 3

blocks.text: **Narrowing** (big type to small type) needs an explicit cast, because data may be lost.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: int to long and long to float are widening, so they are automatic. `5L` to int and `3.0` to int are narrowing and need a cast. A `char` cannot hold a negative value.

blocks.text: Before any arithmetic, Java promotes the operands:

items: If either is `double`, both become `double`.
Else if either is `float`, both become `float`.
Else if either is `long`, both become `long`.
Otherwise **both become `int`**, even `byte + byte` or `char + char`.

blocks.text: If both sides are compile-time constants (literals or `final` variables with constant values) and the result fits, no cast is needed. `byte b = 10 + 20;` compiles.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `a` is not `final`, so `a + b` is an ordinary `int` expression and needs a cast. `b + 3` is a constant (5) that fits in a byte, so line 4 compiles.

steps.prompt: Given `short x`, `float y` and `long z`, what is the type of `x * y + z`?
steps.explanation: `x * y` promotes the short to float, giving a float. float + long is float, because float is the wider of the two. No double is involved, so it never becomes double.

blocks.text: Integer types silently **wrap around** when they overflow. No exception is thrown.

blocks.caption: Wraps to MIN_VALUE; 200 - 256 = -56

blocks.text: Python ints grow as big as needed. Java's `int` wraps from 2,147,483,647 to -2,147,483,648 without any error.
In `long r = a * b;` with int a and b, the multiplication happens in `int` first and may overflow. The result is widened only afterwards.

When you'd rather fail than wrap, use the `Math.*Exact` methods: `addExact`, `subtractExact`, `multiplyExact`, `incrementExact`, `decrementExact` and `negateExact` throw `ArithmeticException` on overflow. Each has an `int` and a `long` overload. `Math.toIntExact(long)` throws if the value doesn't fit in an `int`.

blocks.caption: Prints 2147483648, then ArithmeticException

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `big * big` is computed as an int and overflows before being widened to long. Casting one operand first makes the multiplication `long`, so r2 is 1,000,000,000,000 and the two differ.

blocks.text: int to float and long to double are widening, yet they can **lose precision**: a float keeps only about 7 digits.

blocks.caption: The float really stores 123,456,792

items: `c += 2` and `c++` work on a char (hidden cast).
`char d = c + 1;` does not compile: `c + 1` is an int.

steps.explanation: `c++` moves `x` to `y`. With `""` in the middle, the + becomes String concatenation: `y1`. Without a String, `c + 1` is int math: 121 + 1 = 122.

steps.prompt: Fill the gaps so the code compiles.
steps.explanation: `b * 2` is an int, so it needs a `(byte)` cast to go back into b. 5 billion does not fit in an int, so it needs `L`. `1.5` is a double unless you add `f`.

lessons.title: Wrappers & autoboxing
lessons.summary: Integer and friends, parse vs valueOf, the cache, null traps.

blocks.code:
Integer boxed = 5;  // autoboxing
int plain = boxed;  // unboxing
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(7);        // boxed for you

blocks.text: In Python everything is an object. Java has both primitives and wrapper objects, and they differ: wrappers can be `null`, and `==` compares them by identity.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Autoboxing only boxes to the matching wrapper: an `int` literal cannot become a `Long` (you need `5L`). `"x"` is a String, not a char. Generics cannot use primitives: `List<int>` is not allowed.

items: Bad input such as `"4.2"`, `""` or `" 42"` throws `NumberFormatException`.
`Boolean.parseBoolean("TRUE")` is `true`. Any text other than `true` (ignoring case) gives `false`, with no exception.
`Double.parseDouble("1e3")` is `1000.0`.

options: 13 is printed, then an exception is thrown
steps.explanation: `"12"` parses fine, so `13` is printed. `"1.5"` is not an int, so `parseInt` throws `NumberFormatException` at runtime. The compiler cannot check the contents of a String.

blocks.text: Autoboxing calls `Integer.valueOf`, which reuses cached objects for **-128 to 127**. `==` on two wrappers compares references, not values.

blocks.caption: true / false / true

blocks.text: Compare wrappers with `equals`. If one side of `==` is a primitive, the wrapper is unboxed and values are compared.
`Short`, `Byte`, `Long` and `Character` (0 to 127) cache small values too. `Double` and `Float` do not.

steps.explanation: `x == y` unboxes x because y is a primitive, so it compares values (true). `x == z` compares two different objects (1000 is outside the cache), so it is false.

blocks.caption: false / false / true / true

items: `equals` on a wrapper is `true` only for the **same wrapper class** with the same value.
`big.equals(5)` boxes 5 to an `Integer`, so it is false.
`big == small` does not compile: `Long` and `Integer` are unrelated types.

blocks.text: `new Integer(5)` is deprecated. Use `Integer.valueOf(5)` or autoboxing.

steps.prompt: Given the code, which two expressions are `true`? Choose two.
steps.code:
Long big = 10L;
Integer small = 10;
steps.explanation: `equals` needs the same wrapper class: `10` boxes to Integer and `10L` boxes to Long. `big == 10` unboxes `big` and compares the numbers.

blocks.code:
Integer count = null;
int n = count; // NullPointerException
blocks.caption: Unboxing null fails at runtime

items: Wrappers are **immutable**. `count++` on an `Integer` creates a new object.
`Character.isDigit('7')`, `isLetter`, `isLetterOrDigit`, `isWhitespace`
`Character.isUpperCase('a')` is `false`; `Character.toUpperCase('a')` is `'A'`

blocks.title: isDigit is not just 0-9
blocks.text: `Character.isDigit` is Unicode-aware: it is `true` for any Unicode decimal digit, such as Arabic-Indic `'\u0663'` or full-width `'\uFF15'`, whatever the locale. To accept only ASCII digits, test `c >= '0' && c <= '9'`.

blocks.code:
char c = '\u0663'; // Arabic-Indic three
System.out.println(Character.isDigit(c) + " " + (c >= '0' && c <= '9'));
blocks.caption: Prints true false

options: 5 is printed, then an exception is thrown
steps.explanation: It compiles: `a + b` unboxes both. At runtime, unboxing `null` throws `NullPointerException` after `5` is printed.

steps.prompt: Fill the gaps so the code prints `true 7 A`.
steps.explanation: `isDigit('7')` is true, `parseInt("7")` gives 7, and `toUpperCase('a')` is `'A'`. There is no `parseInteger` method.

lessons.title: The Math class
lessons.summary: round, floor, ceil, pow, random and floating-point surprises.

rows: a double from 0.0 up to, not including, 1.0

blocks.text: `int p = Math.pow(2, 3);` does not compile: `pow` returns a `double` even for int arguments.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `Math.pow` always returns `double`, and a double cannot be stored in an int without a cast. `Math.max(3, 7L)` picks the `long` version, which is fine for a `long`.

blocks.text: `round` rounds .5 **up toward positive infinity**:
Python's `round(2.5)` is 2 (banker's rounding) and `math.floor` returns an int. Java's `Math.round(2.5)` is 3 and `Math.floor` returns a double.

steps.explanation: `Math.round(-3.5)` rounds up to -3 (a long). `Math.ceil(-3.5)` is -3.0 (a double). long + double is a double: -6.0.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `round(float)` returns `int` and `round(double)` returns `long`. `floor` and `ceil` always return `double`, so they need a cast to fit in an int.
`Math.random()` returns a double that is at least 0.0 and **less than** 1.0. It can return 0.0 but never 1.0.

blocks.text: Python raises `ZeroDivisionError` even for `5.0 / 0`. Java only throws for integer division; floating-point division gives `Infinity` or `NaN`.
`NaN` is not equal to anything, not even itself. Test it with `Double.isNaN(x)`.

options: Infinity is printed, then an exception is thrown
An exception is thrown before anything is printed
steps.explanation: `10 / 0.0` is floating-point division, so it gives `Infinity`. `10 / zero` is int division by zero, which throws `ArithmeticException` at runtime.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `0.0 / 0` is NaN, with no exception. NaN is never `==` to anything, even itself, so use `Double.isNaN`.

items: `pow`, `sqrt`, `floor` and `ceil` return `double`.
`round(double)` returns `long`; `round(float)` returns `int`. Halves round toward positive infinity.
`Math.random()` is in [0.0, 1.0).
Integer division by zero throws `ArithmeticException`; floating-point division gives `Infinity` or `NaN`.
Never compare doubles that came from arithmetic with `==`.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Immutability, the pool, == vs equals, key methods and + rules.

blocks.text: A `String` is an object that never changes. Methods return a **new** String.
Python strs are immutable too. But Java uses `s.length()` instead of `len(s)` and `s.charAt(i)` instead of `s[i]`. There are no negative indexes and no slicing: use `substring`.

steps.explanation: Both calls return new Strings that are ignored. `s` still points to the original `"hello"`.

blocks.text: String literals are stored once in the **string pool**. The same literal gives the same object.

blocks.caption: true / false / true / true

items: `new String(...)` always creates a new object.
`intern()` returns the pooled copy.
Constant expressions like `"a" + "b"` are joined at compile time and pooled. Concatenation that uses a non-`final` variable builds a new String at runtime.

blocks.text: Python's `==` compares content. Java's `==` on objects compares identity, like Python's `is`. Use `equals` to compare text.

steps.explanation: `b` is not final, so `b + "b"` is built at runtime as a new object. `d` is a final constant, so `d + "b"` is folded to the literal `"ab"` at compile time and comes from the pool.

steps.prompt: Given the code, which two expressions are `true`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `"Ja" + "va"` is a compile-time constant, so `z` is the pooled `"Java"`, the same object as `x`. `y` is a separate object, so only `equals` matches it. `toString()` on a String returns the same object.

blocks.text: With `String s = "banana";`
`substring(begin, end)` excludes `end`. `charAt(6)` throws an exception, but `substring(6)` returns `""`. `indexOf` returns -1 when nothing is found.

blocks.caption: Prints [, a, , b], 2 and n=5

blocks.title: split, lines and formatted
blocks.text: `split` keeps leading and interior empty strings but **drops trailing** ones. Its argument is a regex, so `"a.b".split(".")` is an empty array. `lines()` gives no empty last line for a trailing line break. `"%s=%d".formatted(...)` (Java 15) does the same as `String.format("%s=%d", ...)`.

steps.explanation: The first `g` is at index 3 and the last is at 10. `substring(3, 10)` includes index 3 and stops before 10: `grammin`.

steps.prompt: Fill the gaps so the code prints `4`.
steps.explanation: The comma is at index 5. `substring(7)` is `"Java"`, and its `length()` is 4. Strings have `length()`, not `size()`.

items: `strip()` removes all Unicode whitespace. `trim()` removes only characters up to the space character, `' '`.
Calls can be chained: `s.strip().toLowerCase().replace("a", "b")`.

blocks.text: `+` runs left to right. Once one side is a String, `+` joins text.
`'a' + 'b'` is int math (195) because neither side is a String yet. `null` concatenates as the text `"null"`.

steps.explanation: Left to right: `1 + 2` is 3 (number math). `3 + "x"` is `"3x"`. From then on everything is joined as text: `"3x1"`, then `"3x12"`.

lessons.title: StringBuilder
lessons.summary: A mutable string: editing methods, chaining, equals and capacity.

blocks.text: `StringBuilder` changes **in place**. Most methods return the same builder (`this`), so calls can be chained.

blocks.caption: Prints Jav4

blocks.text: It is like building a Python list and calling `"".join(...)` at the end. Use it when a String is built step by step, for example in a loop.

blocks.title: StringBuffer
blocks.text: `StringBuffer` is the older twin of `StringBuilder`: the same methods, but each one is `synchronized`, which makes it slower. Prefer `StringBuilder` unless threads share the object. Neither class overrides `equals`, so two builders holding the same text are not `equals`; compare their `toString()` values instead.

steps.explanation: `append` returns the same object, so `a` and `b` point to one builder. Both appends change it.

blocks.text: Each row starts again from `"abcdef"`:

items: Ranges are `[start, end)`: the end index is excluded, just like `substring`.
`delete` and `replace` accept an end index past the length; it is treated as the length.
`charAt`, `indexOf`, `length` and `substring` work as they do on String.

blocks.text: `substring` returns a new **String** and does not change the builder.

steps.explanation: `delete(1, 3)` removes `bc`, leaving `adef`. `insert(2, "XY")` gives `adXYef`. Deleting the last char gives `adXYe`.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `reverse()` returns a `StringBuilder`, not a String. You would need `sb.reverse().toString()`.

blocks.text: StringBuilder does **not** override `equals`, so `equals` works like `==` and compares references.

items: To compare content, use `toString().equals(...)`, `compareTo`, or `String.contentEquals`.
`"abc" == sb` does not compile: String and StringBuilder are unrelated types.
`"abc".equals(sb)` compiles but is `false` (different classes).

steps.prompt: Given the code, which two expressions are `true`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Two builders are two different objects, and `equals` is not overridden, so it compares references. `String.equals` needs another String. `contentEquals` and `toString().equals` compare the characters.

items: `length()` is the number of characters stored.
`capacity()` is the size of the internal buffer. It grows automatically.
`new StringBuilder()` starts with capacity 16.
`new StringBuilder(50)` is empty, with capacity 50. It does **not** contain "50".
`new StringBuilder("hi")` has capacity 16 + 2 = 18.

blocks.text: `charAt(i)` throws an exception for any `i >= length()`, even if `i` is less than the capacity.

steps.explanation: The int argument sets the starting capacity (10), not the content. After appending `hey`, the length is 3. The capacity stays 10 because 3 chars fit.

steps.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `olleh!`.
steps.explanation: Create the builder, add `hello`, reverse it to `olleh`, then add `!` and print. `toUpperCase` is a String method; StringBuilder does not have it.

lessons.title: Text blocks
lessons.summary: Multi-line strings, incidental whitespace and escapes.

blocks.text: A **text block** starts with `"""` followed by a line break and ends with `"""`.

blocks.caption: Quotes need no escaping

items: Nothing except whitespace may follow the opening `"""` on its line.
The result is an ordinary `String`, with all the usual methods.
Text blocks are compile-time constants, so they are pooled like literals.

blocks.text: They look like Python's triple-quoted strings, but Java removes the shared indentation for you and the opening `"""` must end its line. `"""hi"""` on one line does not compile.

steps.code:
String s = """Hello""";
System.out.println(s);
steps.explanation: The opening `"""` must be followed by a line break. Text cannot start on the same line.

blocks.text: Java removes the indentation that **all** content lines share, counting the closing `"""` line too.

blocks.caption: a = "Hi\n", b = "Hi", c = "  Hi\n"

items: Closing `"""` on its own line: the text ends with a newline.
Closing `"""` right after the text: no trailing newline.
Moving the closing `"""` further left adds indentation to every line.

steps.explanation: The smallest indentation is shared by `green` and the closing delimiter, so it is removed. `red` keeps its 2 extra spaces, and the closing `"""` on its own line adds a final newline.

rows: Join with the next line (no newline)
One space that is never stripped

blocks.caption: Spaces shown as _

blocks.text: Trailing spaces at the end of each line are removed silently. Use `\s` to keep one.

blocks.title: Order of processing
blocks.text: The compiler handles a text block in three steps: (1) line breaks become `\n`, (2) incidental indentation and trailing spaces are stripped, (3) escapes are interpreted. In step 2 an escape is still just a backslash and a letter, so `\s` survives the stripping, and an escaped `\n` does not start a new line for indentation purposes.

blocks.caption: One source line, indentation stripped first, then \n becomes a newline

steps.explanation: `\` at the end of a line joins it with the next, giving `ab`. The block ends right after `c\n`, so there is exactly one final newline.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: A text block is always a `String`, even if it looks like a number, so it cannot go into an `int`. Line 2 is fine (plain quotes are allowed) and `\"""` escapes three quotes.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about text blocks are true? Choose two.
options: The opening """ must be followed by a line terminator.
Trailing spaces on each line are kept.
A text block is a String and has all String methods.
The closing """ must be on its own line.
steps.explanation: Trailing spaces are stripped, `\s` is a single space, and the closing delimiter may follow the last text (then there is no trailing newline).
A text block is a compile-time constant, just like a literal. Both are the same pooled `"hi"` object.

items: Opening `"""` then a line break; the closing `"""` decides the trailing newline.
Shared indentation (including the closing line) is removed.
Trailing spaces are stripped; `\s` keeps one space.
`\` at the end of a line joins it with the next line.
A text block is a normal, pooled `String`.

blocks.text: 11 exam-style questions covering the whole unit. Read every line: on the real exam, `Compilation fails` is often the right answer.
For an output question, first check that every line compiles. Then trace the values, and watch for int division, promotion, `++`, the String pool and `==`.

steps.explanation: `x / y` is long division: 5 / 2 = 2. Multiplying by `2.0` promotes to double: 4.0.

steps.prompt: Which three lines compile? Choose three.
steps.explanation: A constant int may go into byte, short or char if it fits: 127 fits a byte, 65 fits a char, and `'a'` (97) fits a short. 128 is too big for a byte, `1.0` is a double, and `10L` is a long.
`concat` returns a new String that is ignored, so `s` stays `Java`. The builder is changed in place to `Java21`.
Like Integer, `Long` caches -128 to 127. Two boxed 100s are the same object; two boxed 200s are not.
`floor(-2.5)` is -3.0. `round(-2.5)` rounds up to -2. -3.0 + -2 is -5.0, a double.
`i++` gives 2 and i becomes 3. 2 * 3 = 6. `--i` makes i 2 and gives 2. So j = 8 and i = 2.
The content is `A`, tab, `B`, newline, two spaces, `C`. The 4-space indentation is removed and there is no trailing newline, so the length is 7.

steps.prompt: Given `String s = "abc";`, which two expressions are `true`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: `substring(1, 2)` is just `"b"`. `charAt(3)` is out of range and throws. `replace` builds a new String at runtime, so `==` against a literal is false.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `s * 2` is an int, so line 2 needs a cast. Line 3 is fine because `*=` includes the cast.
`replace(1, 3, "ab")` swaps `23` for `ab`, giving `1ab45`. Reversed, that is `54ba1`, and index 1 is `4`.
Left to right: `1 + 'a'` is int math, 1 + 97 = 98. Then a String joins in, so `2` and `3` are added as text: `98b23`.
